Scope
-----
This work item focuses on ensuring agents reliably create agent-specific worktrees and branches, persist their work there, and make that work visible across worktrees using the existing Worklog CLI (`wl`) and repo conventions. No changes will be made to Worklog core code in this work item. If the integration tests reveal a Worklog product issue, we will file GitHub issues describing repro steps and suggested fixes.

Primary deliverable
-------------------
An agent skill (code + tests + docs) that: creates a named agent worktree `<agent-name>-<DD-MM-YY-HH-MM>`, creates/checks-out a branch using the repository convention (see `command/implement.md`), commits changes, invokes `wl sync`, and demonstrates that another worktree can see the branch and commit after `wl sync`.

Success criteria
----------------
- The agent skill can be invoked in an ephemeral environment and creates a worktree, creates/checks-out an appropriate branch, commits, and runs `wl sync` without requiring Worklog core changes.
- An integration test harness runs two or more ephemeral worktrees: Agent A runs the skill and `wl sync`; Agent B runs `wl sync` and can see Agent A's branch and commit (matching commit hash and files). Tests must include a basic concurrent-commit detection scenario and record reproducible logs.
- All deliverables include tests, usage docs, and a runbook for triage. When tests surface a Worklog core gap, a GitHub issue with repro steps, logs, and suggested options will be filed.

Out of scope
------------
- Modifying Worklog core source code. Instead, create GitHub issues for product changes.
- SDK changes (these will be considered separately outside this work item).
- Large RBAC/permissions redesigns. If required, file issues and document the required changes.

Deliverables
------------
- `agents/skills/create-worktree-skill/` — agent skill code, unit tests, small example harness demonstrating the happy path.
- `tests/integration/agent-worktree-visibility.sh` — integration harness that runs ephemeral worktrees and asserts visibility.
- `docs/agents-worktrees.md` and `docs/runbook-agent-conflicts.md` — usage, troubleshooting, and GH issue template for reporting product gaps.

Related work

Parent epic: SA-0MKXVC7NA0UQLDR7 (Orchestration)
Related items: SA-0MKXVTHF70EXG01D (Swarmable Plans), SA-0MKXY5Q0Q1UW4P5T (Build to keep Patch going)

Notes

- Branch/worktree conventions: follow `command/implement.md` in this repository for naming and lifecycle rules.
- Backwards compatibility is not required.

Summary:
Design, define, and build an Automated PM Agent (APMA) that acts as a discovery, definition, and delegation engine to coordinate delivery across human and automated sub-agents. The APMA's responsibility is to ensure clarity of plan, break down work into actionable tasks, assign or delegate those tasks, and monitor progress — it does not implement code changes or directly modify repositories.

Goal / Scope:
The APMA intake flow accepts briefs and performs discovery to surface candidate work, creates clear work definitions (analysis, design, implementation spec, test plan, docs), and delegates those tasks to appropriate agents or teams. It sequences and coordinates work, triggers or requests non-destructive checks (builds/tests in read-only mode), and reports status, risks, and blockers. All code or repository modifications are executed by delegated agents (people or automation) under explicit approval policies.

User stories:
- As a product lead, I want the APMA to turn a high-level brief into a clear plan with defined tasks and assignees so work can start without ambiguous follow-ups.
- As an engineer or sub-agent, I want the APMA to produce unambiguous child work-items (analysis, design spec, implementation spec, tests, docs) with acceptance criteria so I can execute my assigned work with minimal additional discovery.
- As a stakeholder, I want the APMA to delegate work to named agents, maintain an audit trail of delegation actions, and produce regular progress reports so I can monitor delivery.
- As a safety officer, I want the APMA to default to read-only discovery and never perform destructive repo operations without explicit separate approval.

Expected behaviour / outcomes:
- The APMA discovers and ranks candidate items from `idea` stage, runs readiness checks, and returns a clear recommended plan with proposed child tasks and suggested assignees/agent-groups.
- The APMA can create draft child work-items or add delegation comments in `wl` to record what should be done and who should do it; it may assign tasks to agent identities but will not perform repository pushes, merges, or direct code edits.
- The APMA coordinates non-destructive operations (CI runs in dry-run mode, linting, static analysis) and attaches results to work-items; any mutating repository actions are delegated and require separate approvals.
- The APMA generates progress summaries (open/blocked items, percent complete, top risks) and maintains an auditable comment trail for decisions and delegations.
- The APMA can also generate new ideas for exploration (research spikes, prototypes, alternative approaches) and surface them as candidate `idea`-stage work-items for further discovery.
- The APMA can respond clearly about the status of any particular work-item or group of work-items, providing current stage, recent activity, assigned agents, blockers, and next recommended actions.

Acceptance criteria:
1) Given a project brief, the APMA creates an epic with child work-items that define discovery tasks, analysis, design, implementation spec, testing, and documentation steps with measurable acceptance criteria in `wl`.
2) The APMA can produce a delegation plan for a selected work-item: a list of proposed child tasks, suggested assignee agent-groups, and the rationale for each delegation (verify: `wl show` and comments reflect proposed tasks and rationale).
3) The APMA provides read-only discovery by default; `propose` or `delegate` actions create draft child work-items or comments but do not modify code repositories. Any `apply` mode that triggers repository changes must be explicitly approved and executed by delegated agents.
4) The APMA produces human-readable progress reports and an audit trail of delegation actions attached to the relevant work-items.

Suggested implementation approach:
- Phase 1 (define): Create PRD, agent responsibilities, safety/permission model, and minimal architecture (core controller + plug-in subagents for wl, delegation, reporting).
- Phase 2 (MVP): Implement intake parser, discovery scorer, task composer, delegation planner (creates draft child work-items and comments), and reporting module. Keep all repo-affecting steps as outputs for delegated agents.
- Phase 3 (operate): Integrate with sub-agents (analysis-agent, design-agent, dev-agent, test-agent), refine delegation mappings, and add audit and reporting enhancements.

Deliverables:
- PRD and design doc stored in the repo describing discovery/definition/delegation model and safety policy.
- APMA components (service/CLI) that implement the MVP acceptance criteria above, but do not perform direct repository mutations.
- Tests validating `wl` creations, proposed delegations, and reporting behavior.

Notes / constraints:
- APMA is non-destructive by default: repository changes are outside its remit and must be performed by delegates under separate approvals.
- Follow repo conventions for task naming, branch suggestions, and commit message drafts; these should be provided as outputs for delegates, not applied by APMA.
- Maintain clear audit logs in work-items when delegations or proposals are created.

Acceptance test steps:
- Run APMA with a sample brief and verify an epic is created with well-defined child tasks: `wl show <epic-id>`.
- Verify the APMA produced a delegation plan and comments suggesting assignees/agent-groups for child tasks.
- Confirm APMA's operations did not perform any repository pushes or merges; repository-affecting steps are present as delegated outputs only.
- Generate the APMA progress report and confirm it lists open/blocked items, percent complete, and top risks.

Related: SA-0ML5E7ZHH0Y5VJQE (select-next-intake-ready-item) and other skills that focus on discovery and delegation.

Summary:
Create a reusable "select-next-intake-ready-item" skill that discovers and defines the next worklog item in the `idea` stage which should be advanced to `intake_complete`, and then delegates the resulting tasks to appropriate sub-agents for execution. This skill is part of the APMA's discovery and planning toolset: it focuses on surfacing ready work, producing clear task definitions, and assigning/delegating those tasks — the APMA coordinates delivery but does not perform the implementation work itself.

Goal:
Provide a deterministic, configurable function/skill that can search worklog (wl) for candidate items, run readiness checks, produce a structured task definition (including acceptance criteria and suggested subtasks), and recommend or delegate the item to one or more sub-agents (e.g., analysis-agent, design-agent, dev-agent, test-agent). The skill must support a read-only discovery mode and a delegation mode that creates the appropriate child work-items or adds delegation comments, but it must not modify code repositories directly.

User stories:
- As the APMA, I want the skill to answer "what should be moved from idea -> intake_complete next?" and return a single work-item id plus a clear plan of what needs to be done and who should do it.
- As an engineer or agent, I want the APMA to produce unambiguous child tasks (analysis, design spec, implementation spec, tests, docs) with acceptance criteria so I can act without extra discovery work.
- As a stakeholder, I want the APMA to delegate tasks to the right sub-agents and provide a communication trail (work-item comments and assignments) so responsibility and progress are clear.
- As a safety officer, I want the APMA to run in read-only mode by default and never perform destructive repository actions — delegation triggers agents who are responsible for code changes under human or delegated policy approvals.

Acceptance criteria:
1) The skill returns a JSON structure with: `id`, `score`, `rationale`, `checks` (list of passed/failed readiness checks), `proposed_tasks` (array of child task definitions), and `action` (suggested: `recommend` | `delegate`).
2) The skill respects filters: only search `idea` stage, allow override tag filters, and allow minimum priority threshold.
3) The skill supports `dry_run` (discovery-only), `propose` (creates draft child work-items in wl but does not assign or change stage), and `delegate` mode (creates/assigns child tasks to named agents or agent-groups; still read-only regarding repositories). Any state changes require explicit approval or delegate policy.
4) The skill includes unit tests mocking `wl` outputs and verifying selection, task-definition, and delegation logic.

Implementation notes:
- Implement as a Python module under `tools/skills/select_next_intake.py` with a thin CLI and a function interface for other agents to call.
- Data access uses `wl` for authoritative state (e.g. `wl list --stage idea --json`) but provide an injectable data-source abstraction for tests and simulations.
- Output includes: readiness checks, scoring breakdown, proposed child tasks (title, description, acceptance criteria, suggested assignee/agent, priority), and a human-readable plan summary.
- Scoring: start simple (priority weight, has_acceptance_criteria, has_assignee, no_open_blockers); expose weights in config.
- Logging: structured logs and a short human-readable rationale; all delegation actions must record comments on work-items describing what was delegated and to whom.

SKILL.md (first draft):

---
# select-next-intake-ready-item Skill

Purpose
- Discover the next worklog item in `idea` stage that is ready to move into intake and produce a clear, actionable plan that can be delegated to sub-agents. The skill focuses on discovery, definition, and delegation — the APMA coordinates work and ensures clarity, but does not directly modify code or repos.

How it works
- Searches worklog for items in `idea` stage.
- Runs readiness checks and computes a score.
- Produces a set of proposed child tasks (analysis, design spec, implementation spec, tests, docs) with acceptance criteria and suggested agent(s).
- Returns the top candidate and either recommends next steps or delegates the proposed tasks to named agents by creating wl child work-items and adding delegation comments.

Usage

Command-line
```
# Dry-run (default): discovery-only, returns recommendation and proposed tasks
python -m tools.skills.select_next_intake --dry-run

# Propose: create draft child work-items in wl (no stage changes)
python -m tools.skills.select_next_intake --propose --config config.yml

# Delegate: create child work-items and assign them to sub-agents (requires --approve or delegate policy)
python -m tools.skills.select_next_intake --delegate --assign-to analysis-agent,dev-agent --approve
```

API (Python)
```
from tools.skills.select_next_intake import select_next

result = select_next(mode='dry_run', filters={"min_priority":"medium"})
# result => {
#   "id": "WL-123",
#   "score": 87,
#   "rationale": "High priority, has acceptance criteria, no blockers",
#   "checks": [ {"name":"has_acceptance_criteria","ok":true}, ... ],
#   "proposed_tasks": [ {"title":"Analysis: scope & gaps", "assignee":"analysis-agent", ... } ],
#   "action": "recommend"
# }
```

Result schema
- id: string (work-item id)
- score: integer (0-100)
- rationale: short human-readable string
- checks: array of {name, ok, details}
- proposed_tasks: array of {title, description, acceptance_criteria, suggested_assignee_or_agent, priority}
- action: `recommend` | `propose` | `delegate`

Configuration
- Accepts JSON/YAML config to adjust scoring weights, filters, and delegation mapping (which tags map to which agent-groups).
- Default weights: weight(priority)=0.5, weight(acceptance)=0.2, weight(assignee)=0.2, weight(blockers)=0.1

Safety model
- Default mode is `dry_run` (read-only).
- `--propose` creates draft child work-items in `wl` but does not change the parent stage.
- `--delegate` assigns tasks to agents and may add delegation comments; it never performs repository pushes/merges. Any repository actions are left to delegated agents and require separate approval.
- All delegation actions are logged as comments on the parent work-item and child items, including timestamp, agent, mode, and rationale.

Testing
- Unit tests for scoring, checks, and proposed_tasks generation.
- Integration tests mocking `wl` outputs to verify that `propose` and `delegate` modes create the expected child items and comments without touching repositories.

Open questions / TODOs
- Finalize delegation mapping (tag -> agent-group) and default assignees.
- Define how to detect and represent "open blockers" in wl (relationships, tags, or explicit blocker fields).
- Define audit trail format for delegation actions and retention policy.

---

data.description:
Process for /plan conflict detection converted to WL CLI commands and helper work-items.

Steps (converted to wl commands):
1) Input: `epic_id`.
2) Fetch siblings: run `wl show <epic_id> --children --json` to obtain canonical workitem JSONs. Each workitem must include an array `allowed_files` (list of exact paths).
3) Normalize: ensure paths are normalized (posix, no trailing slashes) and ignore empty entries (client-side).
4) Grouping: run the detection module `plan.detection.group_overlaps(children)` (local code) to build a path -> [workitems] map.
5) For each path where multiple workitems reference it:
   a) select `blocker_id` = `plan.detection.choose_blocker(items)` (highest `sortIndex`; tie -> earliest `createdAt`).
   b) compute `blocked_ids` = items excluding `blocker_id`.
   c) For each `blocked_id`: perform idempotence checks using dependency records + allowed_files:
      - call `wl dep list <blocked_id> --json` and skip if an existing dep edge points to `blocker_id` and its recorded allowed_files already cover the overlapping paths.
      - if the dep edge does not exist, or exists but does not include the new overlapping paths, proceed to create or update the dependency record and then add comments.
   d) If not present, record the dependency via `wl dep add <blocked_id> <blocker_id> --json` and post comments:
      - on blocked item: `wl comment add <blocked_id> --comment "Blocked by <blocker_id> (paths: <comma-separated paths>)" --json`
      - on blocker item: `wl comment add <blocker_id> --comment "Blocking <blocked_id> (paths: <comma-separated paths>)" --json`
   e) Optionally: set blocked item's status to `blocked` and add tag `blocked` via `wl update <blocked_id> --status blocked --tags "+blocked" --json` (ensure tag merging).
6) Consolidated reporting: after all paths processed, post a summary comment on the epic: `wl comment add <epic_id> --comment "Plan detection summary: <details>" --json`, but only if not already present (use `wl comment list <epic_id> --json` and client-side exact match).
7) Idempotence: all writes (deps/comments/status) are guarded by the above checks to avoid duplicates; re-running `/plan` must be a no-op when no new overlaps exist.
8) Error handling & permissions: failures to write deps/comments must be reported as warnings in the epic comment; partial failures should be retried or surfaced as actionable errors.
9) Tests and CI: provide unit tests that mock the WL CLI and exercise grouping, blocker selection, and idempotence. Provide an integration test that runs `/plan` twice and asserts no duplicate deps/comments.

New helper/CLI work items created to support the conversion:
- SA-0ML6D6UJ21D9XTNU: Add dependency commands to wl CLI (dep-add/dep-list/dep-remove)

Comment formats (exact text used to detect duplicates):
- Blocked comment: `Blocked by <blocker_id> (paths: <comma-separated paths>)`
- Blocker comment: `Blocking <blocked_id> (paths: <comma-separated paths>)`
- Epic summary: `Plan detection summary: <details>`

Notes:
- Uses exact-path matching only (no globs).
- Multiple overlapping paths between the same pair should result in a single dep edge but multiple path entries in comments or a consolidated comment.
- WL CLI helper commands may be extended to support `--json` and exact-match detection convenience operations.

Problem statement
AMPA Daemon: a small Python-based daemon that monitors LLM agent activity and notifies a Discord channel via the Discord bot + Unix socket model. It sends periodic heartbeat notifications (configurable interval) indicating the agent is alive, managed by an integrated scheduler.

Users
- Operators running LLM agents on a single host who need lightweight visibility into agent liveness.
- Agent orchestrators and PM agents that expect simple alive/heartbeat signals for monitoring and basic automation.

Example user stories
- As an operator, I want a daemon I can run on the LLM server that regularly posts an alive message so I can see the agent is running.
- As an APMA integrator, I want the message to provide a concise notification so I can monitor agent health.

Success criteria
- Heartbeat messages are sent to Discord at the configured interval; default is 1 minute (env: AMPA_HEARTBEAT_MINUTES).
- Messages are concise heartbeat notifications (hostname/timestamp are computed internally but intentionally omitted from the Discord payload for simplicity).
- The daemon reads the bot token from env var AMPA_DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN and fails clearly (exit code 2) if not set.
- The service is packaged in a Distrobox development container (debian:stable-slim) for developer workflows; the daemon process itself is managed by `wl ampa start` (Node plugin) which handles process lifecycle. Logs are written to stdout/stderr for host/container logging.

Constraints
- V1 is read-only and only sends notifications; it does not modify repositories or create worklog items.
- Runtime: Python (3.12+ recommended); minimal dependencies.
- Bot token must be supplied via env var AMPA_DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN (security: do not commit secrets).
- Heartbeat interval must be configurable via env var AMPA_HEARTBEAT_MINUTES (integer minutes), default 1.
- The Containerfile produces a Distrobox developer shell (not a standalone production image); the daemon is started via `wl ampa start`.

Existing state
- APMA PRD exists and describes an Automated PM Agent and related skills (see docs/prd/PRD_Automated_PM_Agent_-_end-to-end_project_overseer_(SA-0ML5E2A2V1YILTVR).md).

Desired change
- Implemented: a Python daemon (ampa/daemon.py) that:
  - Reads AMPA_DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN and AMPA_HEARTBEAT_MINUTES from environment.
  - Sends heartbeat notifications via the bot socket model.
  - Logs send attempts and failures to stdout with non-zero exit codes on fatal misconfiguration.
  - Includes an integrated scheduler (ampa/scheduler.py) for periodic command execution.
  - Includes triage audit capability targeting in_review items.
  - Includes retry/backoff, dead-letter handling, health/metrics endpoints.

Related work
- docs/prd/PRD_Automated_PM_Agent_-_end-to-end_project_overseer_(SA-0ML5E2A2V1YILTVR).md

## Implementation Notes (audit 2026-03-01)
Architecture migrated from AMPA_DISCORD_WEBHOOK (HTTP webhook POST) to AMPA_DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN (Discord bot + Unix socket model). Container changed from production Python image to Distrobox dev shell. Message format intentionally simplified. Dead-letter path moved to .worklog/ampa/deadletter.log (project-local). Triage audit targets in_review items with 1-hour cooldown. All children completed and closed.

# Intake Brief: Scheduler Configuration & Schedule Windows

> **Headline:** Add `wl ampa config` CLI and per-command schedule windows so operators can view, persist, and constrain scheduler settings without relying solely on environment variables.

## Problem Statement

The scheduler's runtime configuration (`SchedulerConfig`) is currently read-only from environment variables with hardcoded defaults. There is no way to persist configuration overrides, view the effective configuration at a glance, or constrain individual commands to specific time windows. Operators must set env vars before starting the daemon and have no runtime visibility into what values are active.

## Users

- **Operators/producers** who manage the scheduler daemon and need to tune scheduling behavior (intervals, weights, windows) without restarting the daemon or editing env vars.
  - *User story:* As an operator, I want to run `wl ampa config` to see the effective scheduler configuration so I can verify what values are active without inspecting env vars and code defaults.
  - *User story:* As an operator, I want to run `wl ampa config set poll_interval_seconds 10` to persist a configuration override so the scheduler uses my preferred interval across restarts.
  - *User story:* As an operator, I want to set per-command schedule windows (e.g., only run a command between 09:00-10:00 and 16:00-17:00 on weekdays) so I can control when specific commands are eligible for execution.

## Success Criteria

1. `wl ampa config` (no args) displays all effective configuration values, showing the source of each value (env var, persisted override, or default).
2. `wl ampa config set <key> <value>` persists a configuration override in `scheduler_store.json`; the override takes effect on the next scheduler poll cycle.
3. `wl ampa config reset <key>` removes a persisted override, causing the field to fall back to the env var or default value.
4. `wl ampa config set-window <command-id> --hours '9-10,16-17' --days 'mon-fri'` persists per-command schedule windows in the command's entry in `scheduler_store.json`.
5. Commands outside their configured schedule window are silently skipped during that poll cycle.
6. `wl ampa status` includes an effective configuration summary section.
7. Precedence is: env var > persisted override > hardcoded default. This is documented.
8. Schedule windows are stored in UTC but displayed and accepted in the local timezone.
9. All existing SchedulerConfig fields (poll_interval_seconds, global_min_interval_seconds, priority_weight, store_path, llm_healthcheck_url, max_run_history) are configurable via the new CLI, plus the new per-command window fields.
10. Tests cover: config precedence (env > persisted > default), config persistence round-trip, schedule window evaluation, window skip behavior, and CLI operations.

## Constraints

- Configuration overrides are persisted in the existing `scheduler_store.json` file, extending the pattern established by the Live Promotion Gate toggle (`auto_assign_enabled`).
- Env vars always take precedence over persisted overrides so operators can override at runtime.
- Schedule windows use time-period ranges (e.g., `9-10,16-17`) and day-of-week names (e.g., `mon-fri`). Internally stored as UTC; converted to/from local timezone on input and display.
- The `clear-window` operation is not needed initially; `set-window` with empty values or the general `reset` mechanism can clear windows.
- Team/area scoping is explicitly out of scope for this work item.
- `wl ampa config set` should validate key names against known SchedulerConfig fields and reject unknown keys with a clear error message.
- Changes must be backward-compatible: the scheduler must continue to function correctly with no persisted config (env vars + defaults only).

## Existing State

- `SchedulerConfig` is a frozen dataclass at `ampa/scheduler.py:144-194` with 6 fields, all sourced from env vars via `from_env()`. No disk persistence, no serialization, no round-tripping.
- The Live Promotion Gate (SA-0MLDAXMVV0EQ5XX0) added a single `auto_assign_enabled` toggle stored in `scheduler_store.json`, but no general config surface.
- `wl ampa status` shows daemon process status but no configuration details.
- No `wl ampa config` subcommand exists.
- No per-command schedule windows exist; all commands are globally eligible at all times.
- Env vars: `AMPA_SCHEDULER_POLL_INTERVAL_SECONDS`, `AMPA_SCHEDULER_GLOBAL_MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS`, `AMPA_SCHEDULER_PRIORITY_WEIGHT`, `AMPA_SCHEDULER_MAX_RUN_HISTORY`, `AMPA_LLM_HEALTHCHECK_URL`.
- `ampa/fallback.py` has an analogous `load_config()`/`save_config()` pattern for per-project fallback config that can serve as a reference.

## Desired Change

1. **Config persistence**: Add a `config` key to `scheduler_store.json` to store persisted overrides. Update `SchedulerConfig` (or a companion loader) to read persisted overrides from the store and merge them with env vars and defaults using the precedence: env > persisted > default.
2. **Config CLI**: Add a `wl ampa config` subcommand with operations: show (default), `set <key> <value>`, `reset <key>`, and `set-window <command-id> --hours <ranges> --days <days>`.
3. **Schedule windows**: Add `allowed_hours` and `allowed_days` fields to command entries in the scheduler store. The scheduler's command-selection loop checks these constraints and silently skips commands outside their window.
4. **Status extension**: Add an effective configuration summary section to `wl ampa status` output.
5. **Documentation**: Update `ampa/README.md` and `ampa/scheduler_schema.md` with the new config CLI, persistence model, precedence rules, and schedule window format.

### Key files likely to change
- `ampa/scheduler.py` — `SchedulerConfig`, `SchedulerStore`, command selection logic
- `ampa/scheduler_cli.py` — new `config` subcommand
- `ampa/daemon.py` — status output extension
- `ampa/scheduler_schema.md` — schema documentation
- `ampa/README.md` — operator documentation
- `tests/` — new test files for config and schedule windows

## Risks & Assumptions

### Risks
- **Scope creep**: Per-command windows could expand into full cron-like scheduling, timezone-per-command settings, or team/area scoping. Mitigation: record any additional features discovered during implementation as separate work items linked via `discovered-from:SA-0MLDAXNBQ17OA9PT`.
- **Config drift between store and env**: Operators may forget they have persisted overrides and be confused when env var changes don't take effect (since env wins). Mitigation: `wl ampa config` (show) displays the source of each value, making conflicts visible.
- **Scheduler store corruption**: Writing config to the same `scheduler_store.json` used for command definitions and run history increases the blast radius of a corrupt write. Mitigation: use atomic writes (write-then-rename) and validate JSON before saving, consistent with the existing store write pattern.
- **Timezone conversion errors**: Converting between local timezone and UTC for window storage could introduce off-by-one or DST-related edge cases. Mitigation: use standard library timezone handling (`zoneinfo`/`datetime`) and test with DST-boundary cases.
- **Frozen dataclass compatibility**: `SchedulerConfig` is a frozen dataclass; adding persistence and merging may require changes to how the config object is constructed. Mitigation: keep the dataclass frozen and handle merging in the factory/loader layer, not in the dataclass itself.

### Assumptions
- The existing `scheduler_store.json` write/load mechanism is reliable enough to also store configuration overrides without a separate file.
- `SchedulerConfig.from_env()` can be extended (or wrapped) to accept a store-backed overrides dict without breaking existing callers.
- Local timezone detection via Python's standard library is sufficient; no explicit timezone configuration is needed.
- The `wl ampa config` CLI will be implemented as a plugin subcommand in `scheduler_cli.py`, following the existing CLI registration pattern.

## Related Work

### Work items

- **SA-0MLDAXMVV0EQ5XX0** — Live Promotion Gate & Toggle (completed): introduced the `auto_assign_enabled` toggle persisted in the scheduler store; this work item extends that pattern to general configuration.
- **SA-0MLDAXLDH1TQOYBT** — Candidate Selection Service (completed): the selection logic that config parameters (e.g., `priority_weight`) influence.
- **SA-0MLDAXLVE0JOZ0BH** — Dry-Run Reporting & Notification (completed): reporting that should reflect effective config.
- **SA-0MLDF0YTH01PNA59** — Copy scheduler store config into example (open): downstream item that should be updated after this work lands.
- **SA-0MLJW08I01VIZ6JB** — Add recommendation-aware fallback modes (completed): analogous config persistence pattern in `ampa/fallback.py`.

### Key repository files
- `ampa/scheduler.py` — `SchedulerConfig` class and `from_env()` (lines 144-194).
- `ampa/scheduler_cli.py` — scheduler CLI (641 lines, no config subcommand).
- `ampa/scheduler_schema.md` — env var and scheduling algorithm documentation.
- `ampa/fallback.py` — reference implementation for `load_config()`/`save_config()` pattern.

## Related work (automated report)

The following related work items were discovered by automated search across the worklog and repository. Each item has a direct bearing on the scheduler configuration and persistence changes planned in this work item.

### Additional related work items

- **SA-0MLXELN9J0FCL1K6** — Extract CLI, argument parsing, and output formatting from scheduler into `ampa/scheduler_cli.py` (completed). This item created the `ampa/scheduler_cli.py` module where the new `wl ampa config` subcommand will be added. Understanding the CLI extraction boundaries (what stayed in `scheduler.py` vs what moved to `scheduler_cli.py`) is essential for placing config CLI code correctly.

Established the pattern of configuring scheduler behavior via the `scheduler_store` rather than hardcoded daemon logic. This is a direct precedent for expanding the config surface: it moved operational parameters into the store and demonstrated how `SchedulerConfig.from_env()` resolves the default store path.

- **SA-0MLCRS8O11J2J2DG** — Decide tracking for `ampa/scheduler_store.json` (completed). Decided that the runtime `scheduler_store.json` is gitignored while the example file (`scheduler_store_example.json`) is tracked. This decision directly affects how persisted config overrides are managed: the example file must be updated with new config keys, and operators create their runtime store from the example.

- **SA-0ML7Q2XI11OO3S5I** — Add command scheduling mechanism to APMA daemon (in-progress). The foundational item that created the `Scheduler`, `SchedulerStore`, `CommandSpec`, and eligibility-check infrastructure. The per-command schedule windows (`allowed_hours`, `allowed_days`) extend the `CommandSpec` and eligibility logic introduced here.

Contains integration tests that exercise `SchedulerConfig.from_env()` and `scheduler_store.json` resolution across multiple project directories. Summary

Add a new CLI command `ampa run <command-id>` to run a scheduler command immediately by id and print details about available commands for the current ampa instance.

User story

As an operator I want to run a scheduler command immediately by id and also list available commands with details so I can trigger tasks ad-hoc and inspect available scheduler commands.

Behavior and usage

Usage: worklog ampa run [options] <command-id>

Run a scheduler command immediately by id

Options:
  -V, --version           output the version number
  --json                  Output in JSON format (machine-readable)
  --verbose               Show verbose output including debug messages
  -F, --format <format>   Human display format (choices: concise|normal|full|raw)
  -w, --watch [seconds]   Rerun the command every N seconds (default: 5)
  -h, --help              display help for command

Additionally the command will accept no <command-id> to iterate through the available commands in the current ampa instance and output their details.

Acceptance criteria

1. `ampa run <command-id>` executes the specified scheduler command immediately and returns exit status and output.
2. When `--json` is passed, output is valid JSON with fields: `id`,`name`,`status`,`started_at`,`finished_at`,`exit_code`,`output` (when available), and `instance`.
3. `--format` supports `concise`, `normal`, `full`, `raw` for human-readable output. `concise` shows single-line summaries; `full` shows detailed metadata and output; `raw` prints raw command output only.
4. `--watch N` will re-run the command every N seconds until interrupted (Ctrl+C) and include a timestamp for each run; default watch period is 5 seconds.
5. When invoked without `<command-id>`, the command lists all available scheduler commands in the current ampa instance (supports `--json` and `--format`).
6. Command has unit tests covering: successful run, failing run, JSON output shape, format options, watch behaviour (mocked), and listing commands.
7. Implementation includes integration points to existing scheduler client library and appropriate error handling and logging when `--verbose`.

Suggested implementation notes

- Add new CLI subcommand under `cmd/ampa` or the project's CLI command tree.
- Use existing scheduler client to lookup command by id and trigger execution; if none exists, return a clear non-zero exit code.
- Add tests under `internal/ampa` or `cmd/ampa` test suites; use dependency injection to mock scheduler API.
- Update CLI docs and man-pages; include examples.

Files likely touched (examples):
- cmd/ampa/run.go
- internal/ampa/run_test.go
- pkg/scheduler/client.go (if a client helper is missing)
- docs/cli.md

Notes

If any required scheduler client functions are missing create a child work-item to add client support.

# Intake Brief: Add work-item audit gate to cleanup skill

> **Summary:** Gate the cleanup skill on a work-item audit: when the current branch has an associated work item, invoke the audit skill to verify all acceptance criteria are met before proceeding with branch cleanup, automatically transitioning the item to `in_review` on success or aborting cleanup on failure.

## Problem Statement

The cleanup skill currently only manages branches (inspect, prune, delete) but has no awareness of work-item lifecycle. When a developer runs cleanup on a feature branch that is associated with a work item, the skill should first verify that the work is complete before proceeding with branch cleanup — preventing premature deletion of branches whose associated work items still have unmet acceptance criteria.

## Users

- **Developers running cleanup** — When finishing work on a feature branch, a developer runs the cleanup skill to tidy up. They want assurance that if the branch has an associated work item, the work item's acceptance criteria have been verified before branches are deleted and the work item is transitioned to `in_review`.
- **Project operators/maintainers** — They want a consistent, auditable workflow where cleanup automatically gates on work-item completeness, reducing the chance of closing branches with incomplete work.

### User Stories

- As a developer, I want the cleanup skill to automatically audit the work item associated with my current branch before cleaning up, so that I don't accidentally delete branches with incomplete work.
- As a project maintainer, I want work items to be automatically transitioned to `in_review` when their acceptance criteria are all met and the branch is cleaned up, so that the workflow progresses consistently without manual status updates.

## Success Criteria

1. When the cleanup skill is invoked and the current branch name contains a parseable work-item ID, the skill invokes the audit skill on that work item as the very first step, before any branch operations.
2. If the audit determines all acceptance criteria are `met`, the work item is automatically transitioned to stage `in_review` and the cleanup proceeds with normal branch operations.
3. If the audit determines any acceptance criteria are `unmet` or `partial`, the entire cleanup process is aborted with a clear message explaining which criteria are not satisfied.
4. If the current branch name does not contain a parseable work-item ID (e.g., user is on `main` or a branch without a work-item token), the audit step is skipped and cleanup proceeds normally.
5. The audit step uses the existing audit skill (`skill/audit/SKILL.md`) to perform the work-item assessment — no new audit logic is implemented within the cleanup skill itself.
6. If the work item exists but has no acceptance criteria defined, the audit step should treat this as an abort condition (criteria cannot be verified as met).

## Constraints

- The existing cleanup skill's branch-management steps (inspect, switch, summarize, prune, delete) must remain unchanged in behavior and order.
- The audit skill is invoked as-is; any changes to the audit skill's behavior are out of scope for this item.
- The `inspect_current_branch.py` script already parses a work-item token from the branch name — this existing parsing logic should be reused rather than reimplemented.
- The `do-not-delegate` tag on this work item must be respected; implementation should not be delegated to automated agents.

## Existing State

- The cleanup skill (`skill/cleanup/SKILL.md`) defines a 9-step workflow focused entirely on branch management: inspect current branch, handle uncommitted changes, switch to default, summarize branches, prune local, delete remote, handle edge cases, remove temp files, and produce a final report.
- The audit skill (`skill/audit/SKILL.md`) performs deep code review of work-item acceptance criteria, producing a structured report with `met`/`unmet`/`partial` verdicts and a recommendation on whether the item can be closed.
- The `inspect_current_branch.py` script already parses work-item tokens from branch names (e.g., `wl-SA-XXXXX-description`).
- No existing integration exists between the cleanup skill and work-item lifecycle management.

## Desired Change

- Add a new "Step 0" to the cleanup skill (`SKILL.md`) that:
  1. Checks if the current branch name contains a work-item ID (using the existing parsing from `inspect_current_branch.py`).
  2. If a work-item ID is found, invokes the audit skill on that work item.
  3. If all acceptance criteria are met, automatically transitions the work item to `in_review` stage and proceeds with cleanup.
  4. If any criteria are unmet or partial, aborts the entire cleanup process with an explanation.
  5. If no work-item ID is found, skips this step and proceeds with normal cleanup.
- The change is confined to `skill/cleanup/SKILL.md` — updating the skill instructions to include the new gating step.

## Risks & Assumptions

### Risks

- **Audit skill produces ambiguous results:** The audit skill may return a recommendation that doesn't cleanly map to "all met" vs "any unmet". Mitigation: define a clear decision rule — only proceed if every criterion has verdict `met`; any other verdict (including `partial`) triggers abort.
- **Scope creep:** This item could expand to include reworking how the audit skill reports results, adding new scripted routines, or modifying the audit skill itself. Mitigation: record opportunities for additional features or refactorings as separate work items linked to this one rather than expanding scope.
- **Branch name parsing edge cases:** Some branch names may contain tokens that look like work-item IDs but aren't valid, or the parsing may fail on unusual branch naming patterns. Mitigation: rely on the existing `inspect_current_branch.py` parsing which is already tested; treat parse failures as "no work-item found" (skip audit, proceed normally).

### Assumptions

- The `inspect_current_branch.py` script's work-item token parsing is reliable and covers the branch naming conventions used in this project.
- The audit skill's structured report format (with `met`/`unmet`/`partial` verdicts) is stable and machine-parseable by the agent invoking cleanup.
- The `wl update` command supports transitioning a work item to `in_review` stage from its current status.
- The change is purely to the SKILL.md instructions (agent behavior); no new Python scripts or code changes are required.

## Related work (automated report)

_Generated by find_related skill on 2026-02-24._

### Previously referenced items

- **SA-0MLAJNXE11LPQV66** — "Add scripted routines for cleanup skill" (completed, done): Established the scripted cleanup routine pattern that this item builds upon.
- **SA-0MLWQI6DC09TF7IY** — "Audit integration & lifecycle updates" (completed): Integrated audit skill into lifecycle for work-item state transitions. Provides the model for audit-then-transition that this item replicates inside the cleanup flow.
- **SA-0MLYEOF5J1CXPAJV** — "Implement descriptor-driven audit command handlers" (open): Descriptor-driven audit/close_with_audit handlers — may affect how audits and transitions are invoked in the future. If implemented, the cleanup audit gate could adopt these handlers.
- **SA-0MM02SRD316UW0IN** — "Triage audit should not be operating on in_progress items" (in-progress, critical): Restricts triage audit to `in_review` items — relevant context on audit scope and the stage lifecycle that this item's transition feeds into.

### Newly discovered related items

- **SA-0MLAKDETU13TG4VB** — "Add a scheduler command that will periodically run the cleanup scripts" (completed, done): Established the scheduled cleanup runner that invokes the same scripts (`inspect_current_branch.py`, `prune_local_branches.py`, etc.). Confirms the canonical script set and runner pattern; the audit gate added by this item must not break the scheduler runner path.
- **SA-0ML7OP7L40QKWDB1** — "Mark work-item completed/in_review after merge" (completed, in_review): Defines the same `status=completed, stage=in_review` transition pattern that this item will apply after a successful audit. Ensures the cleanup skill's audit-gate transition is consistent with the implement-flow transition.
- **SA-0MLPYRLRY0ODG6YH** — "AMPA unidirectional delegation, audit, and lifecycle management" (completed, in_review): Defines the overall lifecycle model where audit pass leads to `in_review` transition and `needs-producer-review` flagging. Provides the architectural context for the state transition this item performs.

### Reviewed but not related

- SA-0MLYXXG111QWPTUB (slow cleanup test) — tangential; about test performance, not cleanup workflow.
- SA-0MM0DGYJD11BERV6 (last_audit_datetime) — tangential; optimization for audit cooldown, not cleanup skill.
- SA-0MM0E9LOZ1DBWKFI (remove delegation from triage-audit) — different scope; triage-audit delegation removal, not cleanup skill.
- SA-0MLX8FNGJ0IYN1LN (context assembler) — engine internals, not cleanup skill.
- SA-0MLWQI6HO031F4I3 (validation & tests for engine) — engine validation, not cleanup skill.

### Repository files relevant to this work item

- `skill/cleanup/SKILL.md` — The file to be modified (add Step 0 audit gate).
- `skill/cleanup/scripts/inspect_current_branch.py` — Parses work-item ID from branch name (lines 88-97); reuse this parsing.
- `skill/audit/SKILL.md` — The audit skill to be invoked as-is.

No formal worklog dependencies (inbound or outbound) are registered for this item.

The install-ampa skill (skill/install-ampa/SKILL.md) installs or upgrades the AMPA Worklog plugin but does not pre-warm the container pool. After installation, users must manually discover and run `wl ampa warm-pool` to prepare the pool for fast `start-work` usage.

## Key Design Constraints (from revised PRD)

- **Engine is a one-off command:** Documentation should clearly differentiate between the engine (one-off command processing a work item) and the scheduler (controls when the engine is called).
- **Fire-and-forget delegation:** Sequence diagrams and examples should show independent agent sessions. The engine spawns and exits; agents update work item state on completion.

# Intake Brief: Revisit Delegation Architecture

## Headline

Define a unified execution architecture where the engine owns end-to-end command lifecycle behavior and the scheduler is reduced to a thin execution shell. Deliver an approved architecture decision plus a concrete phased migration plan covering delegation, triage-audit, and all other command types.

## Problem statement

The current boundary between scheduler and engine is inconsistent: both layers contain lifecycle/orchestration responsibilities, and scheduler command-type branching has grown over time. This makes behavior harder to reason about, increases coupling, and slows further refactoring.

## Users

- **AMPA maintainers** need a stable ownership boundary so future command flows can be added without duplicating orchestration in scheduler and engine.
  - User story: As a maintainer, I can implement new command behavior by extending engine-owned lifecycle handling instead of adding scheduler-specific branches.
- **Developers debugging incidents** need predictable control flow and clear ownership of reporting/notifications/recovery behavior.
  - User story: As a developer, I can quickly identify where lifecycle behavior lives and diagnose failures without tracing multiple orchestration layers.
- **Operators using scheduler output** need scheduler behavior to remain simple and focused on execution/reporting presentation.
  - User story: As an operator, I can trust scheduler to execute and present results while engine owns workflow decisions and transitions.

## Success criteria

- A documented architecture decision explicitly defines final ownership boundaries for command lifecycle behavior across all command types.
- The decision includes an explicit target model where scheduler has no command-type-specific orchestration logic beyond dispatch and result presentation.
- A phased migration plan is produced with concrete work-item-sized phases, dependencies, and rollback/compatibility notes.
- The plan maps current scheduler branches and orchestration paths to their target engine-owned equivalents, including delegation and triage-audit flows.
- The plan defines objective completion checks for each phase (tests, behavior parity checks, and code ownership boundaries).

## Constraints

- **Scope:** The decision and migration plan must cover all command types, not only delegation.
- **Deliverable type:** This work item produces an architecture decision and migration plan, not direct code implementation.
- **Priority constraint:** Minimize scheduler complexity and command-type awareness in the target architecture.
- **Compatibility:** Existing externally visible behavior should be preserved unless an explicit and justified deviation is documented in the decision.

## Existing state

- Scheduler currently contains command-type branching (for example delegation and triage-audit paths) and wires multiple orchestration behaviors.
- Engine-side abstractions and handlers exist, but ownership of lifecycle concerns is split across scheduler glue, orchestrator layers, and handler modules.
- Recent refactors moved some audit behavior to descriptor-driven handlers, confirming progress but also exposing remaining architecture boundary ambiguity.
- Prior PRD and workflow docs define execution semantics and validation rules, but implementation ownership is not yet fully normalized to that model.

## Desired change

- Produce a clear architecture decision that defines the scheduler as an execution/presentation shell and engine-owned modules as lifecycle/orchestration owners.
- Define a phased migration model that incrementally removes scheduler command-type branching and transfers lifecycle concerns into engine-owned execution paths.
- Specify interface contracts for unified command execution and result handling so delegation, triage-audit, and other command flows share one consistent execution model.

## Related work

- `SA-0MLYOP9XN1I6P8MX` — current task; architecture boundary decision and migration planning scope.
- `SA-0MLYEOF5J1CXPAJV` — descriptor-driven audit handlers; recent implementation that affects scheduler/engine ownership boundaries.
- `SA-0MLT1ENFV0CTQ1IO` — engine execution semantics PRD; primary architectural reference.
- `SA-0MLX8HGUW0718XI5` — scheduler integration with engine; prior related integration baseline.
- `docs/workflow/engine-prd.md` — canonical execution semantics for lifecycle ownership.
- `docs/workflow/validation-rules.md` — rule constraints that target architecture must continue to satisfy.
- `docs/delegation-control.md` — operational behavior expectations tied to delegation controls.
- `docs/triage-audit.md` — flow documentation likely requiring alignment with the target architecture.

## Risks & assumptions

- **Risk: scope creep across refactors.** Mitigation: capture additional improvements as linked work items instead of expanding this item's scope.
- **Risk: migration ambiguity may create partial ownership splits.** Mitigation: require explicit per-phase ownership boundaries and phase exit criteria.
- **Risk: behavior regressions during migration.** Mitigation: include behavior parity checks and rollback notes for each phase.
- **Assumption:** Existing engine descriptor/invariant infrastructure remains the preferred foundation for unified execution.
- **Assumption:** Team prefers lower scheduler complexity over preserving existing internal layering patterns.

## Related work (automated report)

- **SA-0MLYEOF5J1CXPAJV — Implement descriptor-driven audit command handlers**: This recently changed scheduler ownership by routing triage-audit through descriptor handlers and removing `TriageAuditRunner`, making it a direct precursor to the boundary decision in this item.
- **SA-0MLXEM41U1VIK3TB — Extract delegation orchestration and report generation from scheduler into ampa/delegation.py**: This extraction reduced scheduler size but retained a scheduler-aware orchestration layer, which is exactly the architectural tension this item resolves.
- **SA-0MLXCWZDH0JLL01F — Remove legacy delegation code and eliminate engine/scheduler duplication**: Demonstrates prior dedup efforts and highlights remaining duplication patterns to be addressed in the phased migration plan.
- **SA-0MLT1ENFV0CTQ1IO — PRD: AMPA engine execution semantics & delegation lifecycle**: Canonical design reference for command lifecycle ownership and state-transition semantics that should anchor the architecture decision.
- **SA-0MLX8HGUW0718XI5 — Scheduler integration: replace hard-coded delegation with engine**: Provides practical integration precedent and likely migration constraints for collapsing scheduler command-type branching.
- **docs/workflow/engine-prd.md**: Defines expected command execution semantics and is the primary contract for deciding what belongs in engine versus scheduler.
- **docs/workflow/validation-rules.md**: Captures rule-level constraints that the target architecture must continue to satisfy during migration.
- **docs/triage-audit.md**: Documents a now-stale split that still references legacy flow components; this doc should be reconciled with the new architecture model and migration phases.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Assertions are reproducible: deterministic fixtures with temporary per-project directories; no dependence on machine-specific state.
- Cleanup is reliable: env vars, temp dirs, and any spawned processes are restored/removed after each test.

Final summary
-------------
Replace the engine's PID-based delegation with Podman/Distrobox sandbox containers and integrate with the existing pool manager so agent runs are isolated, traceable by container id, and validated by a CI integration test.

Problem statement
-----------------
The delegation engine currently spawns local opencode processes (tracked by PID) to run agent work. This approach lacks strong isolation, portability, and lifecycle tracking. We need the engine to delegate work by starting prepared sandbox containers, have agents operate inside those containers, and track work by container id until teardown.

Users
-----
- Primary: Developers and engineering teams who rely on reliable, reproducible agent execution for automation and CI tasks.
- Secondary: Product managers and operators who need predictable delegation behaviour and observability.

Example user stories
- As an engineer, I want the engine to run delegated work inside an isolated container so each agent run is reproducible and cannot interfere with the host.
- As an operator, I want delegation tracked by container id so I can monitor, restart, or terminate delegated work reliably.
- As a PM, I want a CI test that validates a full delegation cycle so we can be confident rollout won't break automation flows.

Success criteria
----------------
- The engine can start a prepared sandbox container and launch the agent process inside it; container id is recorded and associated with the work item.
- Delegated work runs end-to-end in the sandbox: tasks can be executed and their outputs observed; at least one sample delegation flow is automated in CI and passes.
- Active work tracking moves from PID to container id; status transitions (started, running, completed, failed) are emitted and stored.
- Containers are torn down when work completes or after a configurable timeout; no orphaned containers remain after normal runs.
- No regressions in existing delegation behaviour; existing opencode process flows are either replaced or mapped to container flows with backwards-compatible observability.
- Suggested verification command (example): run the CI delegation job or locally execute `wl start-work <work-id>`, then `wl list-containers` and `wl finish-work <work-id>` and assert the container is removed and the work item is marked completed.

Constraints
-----------
- Use prepared sandbox container images (existing image likely maintained in a separate Worklog project under ~/projects/Worklog or a container registry). Implementation should locate or accept image names via configuration.
- The project uses Podman and Distrobox for sandboxing; existing pool-management tooling (commands such as `wl start-work`, `wl finish-work`, `wl list-containers`, and `wl warm-pool`) should be leveraged and integrated where appropriate.
- Default: no special network or resource constraints unless later specified; follow repository security policies.
- CI must be able to start containers (runner must support OCI runtimes — podman/docker). The user's CI supports containers.

Existing state
--------------
- Current engine spawns opencode processes directly and tracks them by PID. There is prior work establishing delegation flows and tests (see Related work).
- Work to support container-based delegation has already been started elsewhere: the project uses Podman and Distrobox and contains pool-management code and commands (`wl start-work`, `wl finish-work`, `wl list-containers`, `wl warm-pool`) possibly located in the Worklog project (`~/projects/Worklog`). This intake should integrate with that existing pool manager rather than reimplementing it where feasible.

Desired change
--------------
- Replace the PID-based delegation with a full container-based delegation flow (no backward compatibility required). Specifically, when the engine delegates work it must: (1) acquire or start a sandbox from the existing pool manager (Podman/Distrobox), (2) start the agent process inside the container with a clear payload/IPC contract, (3) record and expose the container id as the primary handle for active work, (4) map lifecycle events (started, running, completed, failed) to work item status, and (5) return the container to the pool or tear it down according to the pool manager policy.
- Integrate with existing pool-management commands (`wl start-work`, `wl finish-work`, `wl list-containers`, `wl warm-pool`) and reuse them where appropriate rather than reimplementing pooling.
- Provide configuration to specify container image, runtime (podman/distrobox), resource limits, and timeouts.
- Add at least one CI integration test that uses the CI runner's container support to validate a full delegation cycle using podman/distrobox and asserts success and proper teardown.

Related work
------------
- command/intake.md — Intake process and where drafts are stored; useful for traceability and the five-stage review flow.
- SA-0MLX8FNGJ0IYN1LN (Context assembler) — maps intake/plan commands to opencode run flows; may have relevant integration notes.
- SA-0MLWQI6DC09TF7IY (Audit Integration & Lifecycle Updates) — intake/architecture notes about lifecycle handling and descriptor-driven handlers.
- SA-0MLZM1VH505B8E22 (Delegation isn't happening) — in-progress critical bug about delegation parsing; review for regressions and test gaps.
- SA-0MLXCWZDH0JLL01F (Remove legacy delegation code) — completed cleanup that may overlap; review commit history and tests.
- .config/opencode/skill/install-ampa/resources/ampa.mjs — contains Podman/Distrobox helper code and checks for required binaries; relevant to container orchestration and distrobox invocation.
- .config/opencode/ampa/Containerfile — example Containerfile and build notes for Podman-based images used by the project.
- .config/opencode/tests/manual/test-devcontainer-e2e.sh — manual e2e script exercising podman/distrobox flows used by local development and tests.
- .config/opencode/tests/node/test-ampa-devcontainer.mjs — test asserting required binaries (podman, distrobox, wl) exist; useful for CI readiness checks.
- .config/opencode/README.md — documentation references for installing podman and distrobox used across developer docs.

Related work (automated report)
--------------------------------
- SA-0MLX8FNGJ0IYN1LN (Context assembler) — maps intake/plan commands to opencode run flows; may describe invocation patterns and helpers that this change should reuse.
- SA-0MLWQI6DC09TF7IY (Audit Integration & Lifecycle Updates) — architecture notes about lifecycle handling and descriptor-driven handlers; relevant for mapping container lifecycle events to work item states.
- SA-0MLZM1VH505B8E22 (Delegation isn't happening) — in-progress bug around delegation parsing and tracking; important to verify tests cover this scenario to avoid regressions.

Risks & assumptions
-------------------
- Risk: Orphaned containers if teardown fails or if the engine crashes during delegation. Mitigation: rely on the existing pool manager's reclaim policies and add CI tests that simulate failures; create a monitoring job to detect stale containers.
- Risk: Secrets or host access leakage from containers if mounts or network policies are misconfigured. Mitigation: avoid mounting sensitive host paths by default; use minimal capability sets and follow existing security policies.
- Risk: Pool manager integration gaps (APIs/command contracts differ). Mitigation: identify the pool manager's command set and add a shim adapter if necessary; create a discovery spike work item if integration is non-trivial.
- Assumption: CI runners support OCI runtimes (podman) — user confirmed this; CI tests will use podman/distrobox.
- Scope creep: Additional features (advanced networking, cross-stage container handoff, metrics) are out of scope for this item and should be recorded as separate child work items.

Investigations / outstanding questions
-----------------------------------
- Confirm exact location of pool-management code and sandbox images/definitions (likely in ~/projects/Worklog). I will search that repository and propose the integration points.
- Confirm CI runner configuration details if further specifics are needed for podman/distrobox (user indicated CI supports containers).
- Confirm pool-management policy decisions: whether to return containers to the warm pool after successful work or to destroy them (default: follow existing pool manager behaviour unless a change is requested).

Suggested next step
-------------------
1) (Recommended) Confirm the sandbox image location and CI runner container support — I will search the Worklog project for image artifacts and propose a candidate; if you confirm an image/registry, I will update the intake and create a CI test template. Example commands I will run: `wl search pool --json`, `rg "wl start-work|wl warm-pool|distrobox|podman" -S` to locate pool manager code and artifacts.

Notes
-----
- Keep scope limited: the initial change should focus on a single end-to-end delegated flow (start container, run agent, observe completion, teardown) and create children work items for further features (e.g., advanced networking, multi-stage container handoff, metrics).

# Add Discord Thread Support to the AMPA Bot

Add a generic threading API to the AMPA bot's notification system so callers can group related Discord messages into threads, starting with test-suite messages.

## Problem Statement

All AMPA bot messages (heartbeats, command results, delegation reports, test outputs) are sent as flat messages to a single Discord text channel. When the test suite runs, it generates many messages (scheduler command outputs, stale delegation recovery notices, etc.) that flood the channel and make it difficult to follow unrelated conversations or find important notifications.

## Users

- **AMPA operators** who monitor the Discord channel for delegation reports, triage summaries, and system health -- they benefit from a cleaner channel where test noise is grouped into collapsible threads.
  - *As an operator, I want test-suite messages grouped into a thread so that the main channel remains readable for actionable notifications.*
- **Developers running the test suite** who want to see test-related Discord output grouped logically per test run rather than interleaved with production notifications.
  - *As a developer, I want each test run's messages in their own thread so I can review a run's output without scrolling through unrelated messages.*
- **Future callers** (delegation, triage, custom commands) who will want to thread their own message groups without protocol changes.
  - *As a module author, I want a simple API parameter to route my messages into a named thread without modifying the bot or socket protocol.*

## Success Criteria

1. The `notify()` API accepts optional `thread_key`, `thread_name`, `thread_silent`, and `thread_auto_archive` parameters that are forwarded through the Unix socket protocol to the bot.
2. When `thread_key` is provided, the bot creates a new Discord thread (or reuses an existing one matching that key) and sends the message inside it.
3. Test-suite messages (those generated during pytest runs exercising the scheduler, delegation, and other components) are grouped into per-run threads named in the format `<command-name> @ <ISO timestamp>` (e.g., `Test Command @ 2026-02-24T10:30:00`).
4. Thread auto-archive duration is configurable per thread via `thread_auto_archive`; if not specified, Discord's default (1 hour) is used.
5. Messages sent with a `thread_key` and `silent=True` (or equivalent) go directly into the thread without a starter message in the main channel. Messages with `silent=False` (the default for non-test threads) post a starter message in the main channel that opens the thread.
6. Test threads default to silent mode (no starter in main channel). Other future thread types default to non-silent (starter message visible in channel).
7. Existing flat-message behavior is preserved for callers that do not pass threading parameters -- no breaking changes.

## Constraints

- **discord.py >= 2.0** is the Discord client library; threading must use its native `Thread`/`create_thread()` API.
- The Unix socket protocol is newline-delimited JSON; new fields must be additive (backward-compatible).
- Thread names are limited to 100 characters by Discord.
- Discord rate limits on thread creation must be considered; the bot should not create excessive threads in a short window.
- The bot process must track active threads (thread_key -> thread_id mapping) in memory; persistence across bot restarts is not required for MVP but the design should not preclude it.

## Existing State

- `ampa/discord_bot.py`: `AMPABot` class sends all messages via `self._channel.send(content=..., view=...)` to a single flat text channel. No thread support exists.
- `ampa/notifications.py`: `notify(title, body, message_type, components)` serializes JSON and sends over a Unix socket. No thread-related fields.
- `ampa/scheduler.py`: Calls `notify()` for command results, test-button messages, and startup messages. Each call is independent with no grouping concept.
- Test suite generates many Discord messages per run (scheduler command outputs, stale delegation recovery, etc.) that flood the channel.
- The socket protocol schema is `{"content": "...", "message_type": "...", "components": [...]}`.

## Desired Change

- **Notification API** (`notifications.py`): Add optional `thread_key: str`, `thread_name: str`, `thread_silent: bool`, and `thread_auto_archive: int` parameters to `notify()`. Serialize these into the socket payload when present.
- **Socket protocol** (`discord_bot.py`): Extend the JSON schema to accept optional `thread_key`, `thread_name`, `thread_silent`, and `thread_auto_archive` fields. When `thread_key` is present, the bot resolves or creates a Discord thread and sends the message there instead of the main channel.
- **Bot thread management**: Maintain an in-memory `dict[str, int]` mapping `thread_key` to Discord thread ID. On first use of a key, create a thread (with the specified name or a default). On subsequent uses, send to the existing thread. Handle archived threads by unarchiving or creating a new one.
- **Test suite integration**: Update the scheduler's test-related `notify()` calls to pass `thread_key=<run-id>`, `thread_name="<command> @ <timestamp>"`, and `thread_silent=True`.
- **Tests**: Add unit tests for thread creation, reuse, silent vs. non-silent modes, and protocol backward compatibility.

## Risks & Assumptions

- **Scope creep**: Threading is initially scoped to test-suite messages only. Additional thread use cases (delegation reports, triage summaries, per-command grouping) should be recorded as separate work items linked to this one rather than expanding this item's scope.
- **Discord rate limits**: Rapid thread creation (e.g., many test runs in quick succession) could hit Discord API rate limits. Mitigation: implement backoff or throttling in the bot's thread-creation path.
- **In-memory thread mapping lost on restart**: The thread_key -> thread_id mapping is in-memory only for MVP. If the bot restarts mid-run, subsequent messages with the same key will create a new thread. This is acceptable for MVP; persistence can be added later if needed.
- **Archived thread reuse**: Discord auto-archives threads after inactivity. The bot must handle the case where a thread_key maps to an archived thread by unarchiving it or creating a new one. Assumption: discord.py's `Thread.edit(archived=False)` is sufficient for unarchiving.
- **Thread name collisions**: Multiple callers could theoretically use the same `thread_key`. Assumption: callers are responsible for choosing unique keys (e.g., including a UUID or run ID).
- **Interaction with SA-0MLXENM2Q08JOQI3**: The open notification refactoring work item may change `notifications.py`. The threading parameters should be designed to survive that refactoring. Mitigation: coordinate if both items are in progress simultaneously.

## Related Work

- SA-0MLXEN5Q91FMXKEB: "Implement Discord bot to replace webhook-based notifications" (completed) -- established the current bot architecture that this feature extends.
- SA-0MM01V1HM0JA8XVL: "Enable Discord bot interactive buttons (MVP)" (completed) -- precedent for extending the socket protocol with new fields (`components`).
- SA-0MLXENM2Q08JOQI3: "Extract and consolidate webhook/notification logic" (open) -- related notification refactoring; threading work should be compatible.
- SA-0MLZUPMD20L99T3C: "Improve delegation report layout using markdown formatting" (open) -- touches Discord message formatting; may eventually benefit from threading.

## Related work (automated report)

### Work Items

- **SA-0MM03WPV801P8Q8Z** -- *Socket Protocol Component Extension* (completed). Direct precedent for this work: extended the Unix socket JSON protocol with an optional `components` field. The threading feature must follow the same additive protocol extension pattern to add `thread_key`, `thread_name`, `thread_silent`, and `thread_auto_archive` fields.

- **SA-0MM03Y5Y41KUITF7** -- *Notification API Component Support* (completed). Extended `notify()` with an optional `components` parameter and serialized it into the socket payload. The threading feature requires the identical pattern: adding optional `thread_key`/`thread_name`/`thread_silent`/`thread_auto_archive` keyword arguments to `notify()` and forwarding them through the socket.

- **SA-0MM03X33703438S8** -- *Bot Button Construction and Sending* (completed). Extended `_send_to_discord()` with an optional `view` parameter and updated `_handle_client()` to pass it downstream. Threading will similarly need to extend `_send_to_discord()` to accept a thread target and modify `_handle_client()` to resolve or create threads before sending.

- **SA-0MLYL6GWK0ED513I** -- *Discord Bot Process Core* (completed). Defines the foundational `AMPABot` class, Unix socket server, `_handle_client()` message parsing, and `_send_to_discord()` method -- all of which will be modified to add thread routing logic.

- **SA-0MLYL6TPJ0Z2DK9U** -- *Notification API* (completed). Established `ampa/notifications.py` with the `notify()` function signature and Unix socket client. The threading parameters will be added to this function's signature and payload construction logic.

- **SA-0MM03YIY609CP27Y** -- *Scheduler Test Button Command* (completed). Demonstrates the `CommandSpec` pattern for auto-registered scheduler commands and how a command calls `notify()` with extended parameters (`components`). The test-suite threading integration will follow this same pattern to pass `thread_key` and `thread_name` from scheduler commands.

### Repository Files

- **`ampa/discord_bot.py`** (lines 330-442). Contains `_handle_client()` which parses incoming socket JSON and `_send_to_discord()` which calls `channel.send()`. Both methods must be extended: `_handle_client()` to extract thread fields from the payload, and `_send_to_discord()` to create/reuse Discord threads via `channel.create_thread()` or send to an existing thread.

- **`ampa/notifications.py`** (lines 187-268). The `notify()` function currently accepts `title`, `body`, `message_type`, `payload`, and `components`. Thread parameters (`thread_key`, `thread_name`, `thread_silent`, `thread_auto_archive`) must be added as optional keyword arguments, and the payload construction block (lines 226-243) must serialize them into the socket message.

- **`ampa/scheduler.py`** (5 `notify()` call sites). The scheduler invokes `notify()` for command results, test-button messages, and startup notifications. Test-suite integration will require updating these call sites (or a subset) to pass `thread_key` and `thread_name` when grouping messages into per-run threads.

Headline

Provide a human-friendly and machine-readable `wl ampa status` summary for the scheduler and discord daemons, with clear health exit codes and a prominent warning if Discord is not configured.

Problem statement

Operators and automation need a reliable, quick way to see the health of AMPA's scheduler and Discord daemons. The current `wl ampa status` output does not explicitly report both daemons' runtime health and configuration warnings in a consistent, machine-parseable form.

Users

- Operators / SRE: run `wl ampa status` to verify both daemons are running and check for configuration issues (e.g., missing tokens).
- Automation / monitoring scripts: call `wl ampa status --json` to integrate daemon health into alerts and dashboards.
- Developers debugging CI/delegation failures: use the command to get a concise one-line status and quick pointers to recent exit codes/logs.

User stories

- As an operator, I can run `wl ampa status` and immediately see whether the scheduler and discord daemons are `running`, `stopped`, or `error` and a short one-line reason.
- As an automation consumer, I can run `wl ampa status --json` and parse structured fields (state, last_heartbeat/uptime, last_exit_code) to determine service health programmatically.
- As a developer, I see a clear warning if AMPA_DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN is unset so I know why discord notifications may be disabled.

Success criteria

- `wl ampa status` prints a human-friendly summary showing scheduler and discord daemon states (each: `running` / `stopped` / `error`) and a one-line status reason.
- `wl ampa status --json` returns structured JSON including at minimum: `name`, `state`, `last_heartbeat` or `uptime` (if available), and `last_exit_code` (if available) for each daemon.
- Exit codes: the command exits with code 0 when all daemons are healthy; exits non-zero when any daemon reports `error` or missing critical config (per policy).
- If AMPA_DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN is not set, the output includes a prominent, human-visible warning and the `--json` output contains `discord_configured: false`.
- Implementation is non-invasive to daemon internals: use existing inspection endpoints/logs or CLI-level checks; no behavioural changes to daemons required.

Constraints

- Non-invasive scope: prefer CLI-formatting and inspection calls; avoid making breaking changes to daemon code or required runtime contracts.
- Must respect existing logging and secrets handling policies (do not print secrets; follow current env var usage).
- Keep backward compatibility: preserve current `wl ampa status` default output semantics where possible while improving clarity.

Existing state

- Repository already contains `ampa/scheduler_cli.py` which formats scheduler-like status lines and codepaths that call `wl status` for startup messages (see `ampa/bot_supervisor.py`).
- Code references and tests exist for discord integration (`ampa/discord_bot.py`, tests under `tests/test_discord_bot.py`) and scheduler state reporting (`ampa/scheduler.py`, `ampa/scheduler_cli.py`).
- There is precedent work handling `wl status` and other `ampa` CLI subcommands (see related work below).

Desired change

- Enhance `wl ampa status` (or the `ampa` subcommand that provides status) to:
  - Print a concise, human-readable status line for both `scheduler` and `discord` daemons.
  - Support a `--json` flag that emits structured health information suitable for automation.
  - Exit with non-zero when any daemon is unhealthy or critical config is missing.
  - Emit a clear warning when the Discord bot token is missing or invalid.

Related work

- Potentially related docs:
  - `command/intake.md` — describes the intake flow and where drafts live; helpful for traceability.
  - `ampa/scheduler_cli.py` — current CLI handling for scheduler status lines and output formatting.
  - `ampa/scheduler_schema.md` — scheduler command descriptors; useful for consistent command naming.
  - `ampa/bot_supervisor.py` — uses `wl status` output for startup messages; shows how status is consumed.

- Potentially related work items:
  - Fix scheduler wl stats command — SA-0ML8XKRV80GORAL7 (addresses scheduler status command bugs).
  - list-containers Subcommand — SA-0MLQ8ZT1300Q1MOM (example CLI subcommand with structured output semantics).
  - Ensure executor always clears running flag on errors/timeouts — SA-0MLGGHJ5B0QQJ4OL (related to exit/health states reporting).

Notes / open questions for reviewer

- Confirm the daemons to include: I have used `scheduler` and `discord` per the title. Are there any additional AMPA daemons/processes you want reported by this command?
- Confirm the exit-code policy: should the command exit non-zero when any daemon is not `running` (recommended), or only for explicit `error` states?
- Confirm we must avoid any changes to daemon internals; if you prefer adding small health endpoints to daemons to improve reliability, say so and we will re-scope.

Related work (automated report)

- Fix scheduler wl stats command — SA-0ML8XKRV80GORAL7 — Fixes scheduler status command bugs which overlap with CLI status output.
- list-containers Subcommand — SA-0MLQ8ZT1300Q1MOM — Example of a CLI subcommand offering structured output semantics that can guide `--json` design.
- Ensure executor always clears running flag on errors/timeouts — SA-0MLGGHJ5B0QQJ4OL — Related to accurate exit/status reporting for scheduler-run tasks.
